speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a letter from Denise North of Richmond, B.C., and I would like to share a part of it with the House. She writes:
This letter is concerning the 29-cent stamp that was issued at Christmas, as it can be used only on envelopes that have a matrix imprinted on.
This is unfair to a lot of Canadians who already have their cards from last year or from organizations who haven't taken part.
In the past few weeks we have seen supermailboxes that open easily, keys that fit all boxes, and now tick and stamp envelopes. When will Canada Post take the delivery of mail seriously and stop creating two classes of citizens? Some Canadians can send Christmas cards for 29 cents, and some Canadians have to send Christmas cards for 34 cents. Why can a 29-cent Christmas stamp not simply be a 29-cent Christmas stamp without having to buy a special envelope that ticks?

Mr. Speaker, airport safety is of great concern to the people of London- Middlesex and indeed to all Canadians. Safety has been the cornerstone of all the Government's transportation initiatives. No stone has been left unturned.
The crash firefighting rescue service standards set by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) exceed the standards set by the ICAO. In fact Canadian standards are more stringent than those of the Federal Aviation Authority of the United States. A regular monitoring system of the people and equipment to do the job is in place. Category levels of service are appraised annually.
[DOT] (U05)
London airport will receive the new rapid-intervention vehicle which has both dry chemical and foam firefighting
capabilities. Our Government is committed to safety. We will have the highest standards of people and equipment. As far as this Member of Parliament is concerned, safety at the London airport will not be compromised.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT RURAL SERVICE NOT BE CHANGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Post project designed to curtail rural services drastically has shaken the 30 per cent of Canadians who live and work outside cities and urban areas. Canada Post intends to close 1,700 rural post offices and privatize 3,500 more over the next five years.
The Canada Post legislative mandate is to provide services to Canadians, no matter where they live. Whereas Canada Post is attempting to do away with rural routes; whereas a clan of Conservatives is trying to flout parliamentary traditions by holding secret meetings on this issue; and whereas the Prime Minister is giving us vague assurances that rural mail will not be wrecked, Canadian men and women serviced through Canada Post rural deliveries insist that such services be maintained as a matter of right.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House a matter of great concern not only to my constituents but to all those producers in western Canada who sold high quality No. 1 and No. 2 wheat during the crop year which ended July 31, 1986. The Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board indicated recently that there may have been some cross-subsidization of prices and, as a result, there is little likelihood of a final payment on the wheat sold during that time.
Since higher grades were sold at a significant premium to the initial prices throughout the crop year, this is not acceptable to producers of those grades. The objective of the pooling

December 12, 1986
system is to provide a producer with the average yearly price of the commodity he delivers, not to ensure a common return to all producers. I call on the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board to review this matter thoroughly in order to ensure that producers are treated fairly in this instance, as well as to set policy for the future.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REIMBURSEMENT OF RETIREES AND EARLY RETIREES FROM 1985
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, older workers in Quebec and throughout the rest of Canada are ever more disappointed by this Conservative Government. I can say that the elderly people who came here to defend the interests of older workers in Quebec left disillusioned. Next Tuesday, in Quebec City there will be a general meeting of all older people who have been victimized by unemployment insurance benefit cut-backs. Similar rallies are scheduled for Montreal, Trois-Rivieres, and the Lac-Saint-Jean region.
Quebecers will form a common front to support all retirees and all the 1985 early retirees who are seeking a full repayment of the money owed to them, and to fight against the Government's impending legislation under which there would be two classes of older citizens, to the extent that some of them would not be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits while they are looking for other work.

[DOT] (mo)

Mr. Speaker, on December 4, 1986, Israeli soldiers put up barricades to the entrance of Birzeit University on the West Bank. The Palestinian students protested the erection of the barricades with a sit-in. The Israelis shot two students, and violence erupted for 8 days. The end result was that 4 students were killed, 5 are missing, 52 were wounded, and 500 Palestinians were detained by the Israeli occupation forces.
Canada, with its track record as a mediator for peaceful solutions to international problems, should support the call for an immediate international conference on Palestine so as to correct the long-standing injustices to the Palestinian people.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF PLANT GENETIC RESOURCE CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just as environmentalists in Canada are trying to protect endangered species of wildlife, plant geneticists at Agriculture Canada are trying to protect Canada's dwindling plant resources which are at risk because the Government has delivered severe cut-backs to agricultural research. The cutbacks last year, and further cut-backs of 22 per cent for 198687, have not only forced the Plant Genetic Resource Centre to ignore domestic plant varieties, but have also put our international collections in danger.
Canada holds the world's principal base collections of oats and barley, but it could face embarrassment because it is not taking proper care of its international collections.
When Dr. Charles Bishop, Canada's representative on the International Board for Plant Genetic Resources under FAO, complained to Dr. LeRoux, the then Assistant Deputy Minister of Agriculture, he was told that the level of technical support and storage capacity at Canada's Plant Genetic Resource Centre "has never been adequate and has in fact regressed over the past three years as a result of major budgetary cut-backs in our branch". These cut-backs must cease.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF PUBLIC SECURITY FORCE OF DRUMMONDVILLE, QUE.
TRIBUTE TO CERTAIN MEMBERS OF PUBLIC SECURITY FORCE OF DRUMMONDVILLE, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to draw the attention of the House to some deserving members of the Drummondville police force. First of all, last June, the Governor General, the Right Hon. Jeanne Sauve, awarded the medal for bravery to Rejean Paul-Hus.
Last week, acting on behalf of the Solicitor General and the Governor General, I awarded the police medal for distinguished service to 29 members of the Drummondville police force. This medal is awarded for outstanding service, to express the community's recognition for services rendered in high-risk areas.
These peace officers have demonstrated their ability to enforce law and order and their conviction: Justice for all.
I welcome this opportunity to pay tribute to individuals who have such distinguished record and who are dedicated to protecting the lives of their fellow citizens.
December 12, 1986

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCUSSIONS AT IN CAMERA COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Tories are a strange lot!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCUSSIONS AT IN CAMERA COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext: Not as strange as you are.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCUSSIONS AT IN CAMERA COMMITTEE MEETING
speechtext:
It would appear that yesterday in a Tory meeting one of the Tory members of the secret committee to discuss postal issues decided to "stool" on everybody else and to reveal what had gone on at the committee. Here is what the Conservatives in majority, seemingly less one, the one who probably stooled on the others, had to conclude: That Canada Post had made no attempts to interfere with Government plans to raise a first-class postage stamp to 36 cents; that rural post offices should be turned over to the private sector; that group mailboxes are supermailboxes, as some people dare call them, and they should remain; that large publications now benefiting from postal subsidies should lose them.
This appears to be a somewhat quasi-unanimous opinion of the Tory members on that committee. I wonder what the end report will look like. I wonder what the Tory who leaked it will look like once the others get hold of him.

Mr. Speaker, in 1979 over 51,000 Jews were allowed to emigrate from Russia. For the last several years barely 100 Jews a month have been permitted to leave. In place of numbers the Soviet Union has adopted a cruel ploy of releasing high profile refusniks to mislead the world into thinking the U.S.S.R. is compassionate.
Nine months ago on February 11,	1986, Anatoly
Shcharansky was allowed to leave Russia and join his wife, Avital, in Israel. We were thrilled by this news. However, we were deeply saddened to hear two days ago that Anatoly Marchenko, who was a member of the disbanded Helsinki Watch Group, died in prison. He had been imprisoned in Russia for over 20 years as a penalty for his fight for human rights.
The Soviet Union needs to be condemned in the strongest possible terms for its flagrant disregard of the human rights Accords it has signed.

Mr. Speaker, after months of indecision, the Government announced the Special Canadian Grains Program which has greatly disappointed western farmers.
As reported in the Winnipeg Free Press on Wednesday, December 10, Bob Douglas, spokesperson for the Keystone Agriculture Producers of Manitoba, a large farm lobby group, said that he was disappointed and that he expected a severe reaction from farmers.
In an editorial in yesterday's edition of the Winnipeg Free Press, the following was reported:
It took months for Prime Minister Brian Mulroney's Cabinet to decide how it was going to face up to its responsibility to assist western agriculture. When the equivocation ended, the Prime Minister used the distress of western farmers as a political tool-
With regard to the delay in the distribution of dollars, the Winnipeg Free Press editorial went on to indicate:
Mr. Mulroney has no problem rolling aside such stones when he wants to corrupt the federal bidding process or to move a jail, at immense cost, to his own riding.
If I may add my own words, money was always found to bail out banks and to support unknown bank depositors. Money is going to pay off investors in the Bank of British Columbia, and capital gains will be 100 per cent tax-free for many investors. Why do our farmers deserve less?

Mr. Speaker, the announcement last Wednesday by the Minister responsible for CMHC of the first issue of National Housing Act mortgage backed securities was a milestone in the history of residential dwelling finance in Canada.
The advantages of Canadian equivalents of the popular United States "Ginnie Maes" include the mobilization of further funds into residential construction, the stabilization of mortgage interest rates, and the creation of an attractive senior investment vehicle for both individuals and institutions.
As expected, once a vibrant secondary market and perhaps even a futures market develop, liquidity will be enhanced.
Congratulations are due to the Government, CMHC, and the involved financial institutions for their initiative in creating the new tradable mortgage backed securities guaranteed in terms of timely monthly payments.

December 12, 1986

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES SALE OF ARMS TO IRAN-ROLE OF RCMP IN INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday in Question Period the Minister for International Trade replied to my questions about the Canadian connection to the arms to Iran affair by saying:
-I can assure the Hon. Member that this issue is being thoroughly investigated.
After Question Period and later in the day, RCMP spokesman Belanger apparently told the press the following: "There is no investigation in this matter. There is no file on this matter. No one asked us to start an investigation". Would the Deputy Prime Minister explain the contradiction between what the Minister for International Trade told me and what RCMP spokesman Belanger told the press later in the day? Exactly what is the RCMP doing in this matter? Who is carrying out the investigation? What has the Government found out so far? In short, why is the Government apparently so much in the dark about the Canadian connection in this arms to Iran affair?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR NAMES OF CANADIANS ALLEGEDLY INVOLVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what should worry the Canadian people is that everybody, including the press, already seems to know more about this matter than the Government.
It has been reported that External Affairs now knows the names of some of the Canadians involved in the Canadian connection to this arms to Iran affair. Will the Deputy Prime Minister give Parliament and, therefore, the public, the names now? Will he also tell us why the Government in its laxity in this matter appears to be condoning the actions of Canadians, directly contrary to Canadian Government policy against the export of arms to a country like Iran? Will the Deputy Prime Minister answer this definite question?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED EXISTENCE OF SECRET STUDY-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for cutting unemployment insurance benefits in Canada. Mr. Speaker, on December 5, when I asked the Minister about the study by Mr. Dickinson on the annualization of unemployment insurance programs, the Minister, and I am quoting Hansard, answered that he was not aware of the study and that perhaps it was the Forget Commission.
I have before me today this secret study that was submitted to the Government in July 1985. I would like to know why the Minister was not aware of the existence of a study that is important to the reform of unemployment insurance programs and why he did not say so at the time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED EXISTENCE OF SECRET STUDY-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question of unemployment insurance, as the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie knows perfectly well, was examined from May or June 1985 to November 1986. During that period, dozens of documents were submitted, either to the Forget Commission directly or to the commissioners, at their request, and these studies were used by the Forget Commission in making its recommendations. The Minister of Employment and Immigration can hardly be expected to know every single document produced in the Department or at the request of commissions of inquiry on specific subjects.

Mr. Speaker, I have to say the Minister is not running his department. The secret study I referred to was carried out between November 1984 and July 1985, and if we look at the report on the study, it is identical to one of the recommendations of the Forget Commission. So I still wonder why today, the Minister, who is responsible for an area that is particularly important to Canadians, is not aware of this study. Who is running the Department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the trouble with the Hon. Member is that he always sees a connection between a document and the way a department is managed. Running a department involves more than being aware or not of the existence of a specific document. The document is part of a range of references the department and the Commission may use in drafting a report and recommendations on a subject that will be examined by the Government and on which we shall be making recommendations in May 1987, as I have said before.

December 12, 1986
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES SALE OF ARMS TO IRAN-U.S.-CANADIAN INFORMATION PROCESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister with regard to the allegations of a possible Canadian connection to the arms sale to Iran. Can the Deputy Prime Minister inform the House that he is satisfied with the process which occurred through which we did not find out anything about this until several hours after it had become public in the United States? Does he think there should have been information given by the American Government or the CIA to Canadian officials, perhaps the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, beforehand? Is the Deputy Prime Minister satisfied with the process? After all, we are a sovereign country and an independent nation. I think we should have been informed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES SALE OF ARMS TO IRAN-U.S.-CANADIAN INFORMATION PROCESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought I answered that question. The answer is no. We have made our expressions of dissatisfaction to this effect to the United States.

Mr. Speaker, since the Deputy Prime Minister said that the Government has expressed its concern to the United States, will he explain whether it has sent a letter of protest to the American officials? If not, is it planning to send a letter of protest to the U.S. officials so that this does not happen again?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said that we have expressed our concern over the way this matter has been handled. This is the fourth time I have answered that question.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I was very pleased to see the Government's concern about corporate concentration as mentioned in the recent Speech from the Throne. In an article in this week's Maclean's, the chairman of one of Canada's largest banks lashed out at corporate takeovers. What specific action will our Government initiate to examine the awesome problem of concentration of wealth in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe it is worth pointing out that the Competition Act that was passed in June now makes it possible for the Government to annul any mergers that have a detrimental effect on competition in the market-place. Second, the Green Paper on financial institutions, written by the Minister of State for Finance, and the Standing Committee study will undoubtedly lead to legislation that will have an important bearing in the area of financial institutions. Finally, my officials are working on this subject to see if there are other changes we could make to the Canada Business Corporations Act. I understand that the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs is looking at corporate concentration as one of its items for study this term. I think that is an excellent idea.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It concerns what I understand to be a secret document, entitled "Option for Change", prepared by Mr. Dickinson. In spite of previous attempts by the Minister to divorce himself from the Forget Commission Report and the recommendation concerning annualization, will he explain the coincidence that the same annualization scheme of Mr. Forget is the one that Mr. Dickinson prepared for his Department one and a half years ago, and which is in the document that I have in my hand? Can he explain that coincidence to the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell never fails to be impressed whenever he spots the word "secret" on a document. It does seem to disturb him. I can only tell him what I told his colleague earlier: lots of documents are produced within the Department. As to whether there might be a coincidence or any kind of connection between this document and the Forget Commission recommendations, the Government is not called upon to do anything. It is quite possible that-I have just received the document mentioned by my colleague opposite-Mr. Forget has drawn inspiration from it, but Government policy is not involved at all. For the third time today I repeat that we will make recommendations in May, and until then we will familiarize ourselves with documents of every description, including some which are no longer secret.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF FORGET REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS
REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF FORGET REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is obvious is that Mr. Forget not only drew
December 12, 1986

inspiration from this report, but he also copied parts of it. So can the Minister tell the House how it is that a recommendation which absolutely no-one, no witness claims to have made but which originated from his Department via this report ended up among those advocated in the Forget Commission study? Why is he still trying to divorce himself from this recommendation, which happens to be his own?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF FORGET REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may use words with which the Hon. Member is familiar, he has been unable to uncover a connection between the document and myself, he has established a connection with Mr. Forget. If Mr. Forget saw fit to include it in his report he did not seek permission from the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He quite simply decided to use that document. As I said, we will refer to it at the appropriate time, in May next year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is a myth that the wage gap for women is improving. When one examines the statistics closely, they show that full-time and part-time working women, taken together, usually earn only 57 cents for every dollar earned by men. What does the Minister intend to do about the increasing trend to low paid, unprotected part-time jobs into which increasing numbers of women are being forced? This means they are being forced into poverty.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find the question asked by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East interesting. You know that jointly with the Department of State for the Status of Women, we are examining thoroughly the whole question of women's salaries, women's income and whatever substantial efforts we want to make to improve on women's employment conditions and income.
I think that in the past two years, there have been very clear-cut improvements in the contribution of women on the labour market as well as in their income level.
However, it is obvious that we were far behind and that very few things were done before us. Moreover, we are quite encouraged at present and we will keep doing our job.

Mr. Speaker, since privatization, down-sizing, and contracting out, which
Oral Questions
are policies of the Government, are threatening full-time jobs particularly for women, what steps will the Minister and his colleague, the Minister responsible for the status of women, take to ensure that full-time jobs presently held by women, particularly in the federal jurisdiction, will not be lost? We are very concerned that they will be lost as a result of these federal government policies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of part-time jobs is a very complex, one especially since there are some jobs available in both the private and public sectors. Many women prefer that type of employment because again it is easier for them to fit into this combination.
Now the Government is trying to implement-through job creation procedures-the employment strategy, especially women's re-entry on the labour market whenever it is possible or they want it so. We are trying to create a market for fulltime jobs but it is a step by step process.

subsubtopic: GEORGES BANKS-EFFECT OF PROPOSED OIL DRILLING ON FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He will know that Texaco Canada Resources is proposing to drill exploratory wells in Georges Banks, some of the world's most lucrative fishing grounds. He will further know that the fishing industry and community have expressed grave reservations about such a proposal. Will he indicate to the House his views on this most controversial subject?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: GEORGES BANKS-EFFECT OF PROPOSED OIL DRILLING ON FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the concern of the Hon. Member for South West Nova is obvious because the livelihood of hundreds of fishermen living in this area could well be negatively affected if appropriate precautions were not taken in regard to any drilling proposals on Georges Banks. Until I receive specific technical proposals from Texaco, and the report of the Gulf of Maine Advisory Committee which advises me on this issue, we are not prepared to approve any proposals for drilling on Georges Banks.

December 12, 1986
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for Canada Post. This morning I received a letter from Denise North of Richmond, British Columbia. The letter concerns the 29-cent stamp that was issued for Christmas and which can only be used on envelopes that have a matrix imprinted on them. This is unfair to many Canadians who already have their Christmas cards. Will the Minister tell Denise North, and thousands of other angry Canadians who cannot use the 29-cent stamp to mail their Christmas cards, why a 29-cent stamp is not like any other stamp, and why it is not available to all Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is referring to a program that was put in place in 1985 by Canada Post, in partnership with the Greeting Cards Association of Canada, including such groups as UNICEF. The program is aimed at using standardized envelopes which may be processed faster and in a more economical way by Canada Post. The money saved in doing this is given back to the clients of Canada Post through the offering of the 29-cent stamp. I guess it is to the advantage of Canadians who can use it.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHY CREATION OF TWO CLASSES OF CITIZENS WAS PERMITTED
INQUIRY WHY CREATION OF TWO CLASSES OF CITIZENS WAS PERMITTED
speechtext:
According to the letter, Mr. Speaker, this service is not available to all Canadians and, apparently, only a few companies produce this envelope, and both the card and the envelope must be bought at the same time.
I do have a supplementary question. Why does the Minister allow Canada Post to create two classes of citizens, namely those fortunate enough to mail a Christmas card for 29 cents, and others who must pay 34 cents? Does that reflect the Canada Post Christmas spirit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: INQUIRY WHY CREATION OF TWO CLASSES OF CITIZENS WAS PERMITTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am trying to make the Hon. Member understand that envelopes are standardized under this program. They are sorted by optical scanners, so Canada Post can save money and pass such savings on to its customers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the Deputy Prime Minister relates to his earlier answer. He said a protest has been made to the United States with respect to this Canadian connection. What kind of protest was made?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROTEST MADE TO UNITED STATES ON ALLEGED CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN ARMS SALE

subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROTEST MADE TO UNITED STATES ON ALLEGED CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN ARMS SALE

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INQUIRY CONCERNING PROTEST MADE TO UNITED STATES ON ALLEGED CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN ARMS SALE

Will the Deputy Prime Minister please come clean with the House and tell us at least-this information-what kind of protest has been communicated to the United States on this serious matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: INQUIRY HOW GOVERNMENT CAN PRESERVE QUALITY AND QUANTITY OF SERVICES WHILE CUTTING PROFESSIONAL STAFF IN HALF
speechtext:
The
President of the Treasury Board being absent, Mr. Speaker, I will direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Yesterday, the President of the Treasury Board stated in the House, and I quote:
With respect to linguistic training, the Government is still fully aware of the need for this program. We are trying to make it more effective and more properly geared to the requirements of our employees.
December 12, 1986

Yet, Mr. Speaker, the Government announced on November 27 to civil servants and language teachers that it was planning to cut as many as 325 person-years from a total of 703 person-years, a cut of nearly 50 per cent.
How can the Government expect us to believe that it will maintain the quality and quantity of services, while cutting half of the professional staff?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: INQUIRY HOW GOVERNMENT CAN PRESERVE QUALITY AND QUANTITY OF SERVICES WHILE CUTTING PROFESSIONAL STAFF IN HALF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could assist the Hon. Member in the absence of the President of the Treasury Board. As the Hon. Member well knows, we have under review a Bill dealing with language, which Bill may assist and meet the concerns registered by the Hon. Member.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

Mr. Speaker, I will repeat my question which has nothing to do with the law pertaining to official languages. It has to do with cutting language training courses.
On November 27 the Department announced that 325 person-years would be cut from the 700 or so people who perform this training at this time. How can one entertain the idea that we will improve, as the Minister told me yesterday, the quality and quantity of teaching when half of the teachers are being cut from the system?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORECAST OF NATURAL GAS RESERVES
NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORECAST OF NATURAL GAS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources I will address my question to the Parliamentary Secretary, who I am sure will be pleased to answer.
Are the Parliamentary Secretary and the Government aware that this week the National Energy Board released a report on supply and demand up to the year 2005? The report reveals what we all know, that is, we are running out of sweet light crude oil. The report also includes the stunning revelation that in 15 years-in the year 2002-we will be running out of conventional natural gas. Does the Parliamentary Secretary remember when we were told that we had 300 years' supply? Is the Government aware of this and, if so, why is it taking steps to make it easier and not more difficult to export all our good easy-to-get Canadian natural gas?
Oral Questions

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD FORECAST OF NATURAL GAS RESERVES

Member.

Why is the Government removing safeguards, for example the gas surplus tests, rather than putting into place protections and policies so that Canadians will have easily accessible, cheap natural gas in the future?

Member that he is a member of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources and that the committee is also studying the very serious questions outlined in the report.

-we have been able to accommodate more than twice the number of households-than any other Government had been able to do in the history of Canada.
From 1981 to 1985 the co-operative housing sector built 5,500 units per year. If the Minister's program is so great will he tell us why not one single unit of co-operative housing has been built this year?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHY GOVERNMENT HAS NOT YET AUTHORIZED PURCHASE OF ROLLING STOCK INCOME TAX CAPITAL GAINS EXEMPTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance. We have learned that the Income Tax Act which will be coming before the House again allows capital gains covered by the lifetime capital gains tax exemption to be exempted from the alternative minimum tax. Can the Minister explain why wealthy Canadians should not pay minimum tax on capital gains and why the Government is giving this Christmas gift to the rich when unemployed Canadians have no pay cheques to look forward to at Christmas?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHY GOVERNMENT HAS NOT YET AUTHORIZED PURCHASE OF ROLLING STOCK INCOME TAX CAPITAL GAINS EXEMPTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has stated only half of the situation. For the purpose of calculating the alternative minimum tax, capital gains will be put in income at the full rate and not be given the 50 per cent deduction. The alternative minimum tax will be calculated after that. The division in half of capital gains which ordinary people can do will not occur under the alternative minimum tax.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is telling us that capital gains will get special treatment and if taxed at all will be taxed at half of the minimum tax rate for everything else. Why do the deductions from income in calculating the minimum tax allow people deductions when they have taken the vow of perpetual poverty, made charitable donations and paid medical expenses and, lumped in with those things which are socially worth while, provide another exemption so that people will pay less on capital gains? What kind of gift is that?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. Could he inform the House why his Government has yet to authorize VIA Rail to purchase the rolling stock it so badly needs if it is to provide an adequate service to railway passengers?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED WITHHOLDING OF INFORMATION-SALE OF BANK OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
The Chair will now make a ruling on a matter raised on December 1 by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). The Hon. Member presented a well reasoned argument relating to the legislation recently adopted to permit the takeover of the Bank of British Columbia by the Hongkong Bank. He also provided me with additional information by way of documentary material. I thank him for so doing.
The Hon. Member alleged that during the debate on the legislation in this House, certain information was withheld. He also complained that information which had been provided to a committee of the other place had not been made available to this House. The Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) assured the House that no information was intentionally withheld. We are therefore faced with an argument as to whether information was withheld or not.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, together with certain other Hon. Members, feel that they have a grievance because, having co-operated in expediting the passage of the legislation in question, they were not as fully informed of the facts as they should have been. The Hon. Minister of Finance does not accept that the grievance is well founded. He maintains that Ministers dealt with all questions raised in committees of both Houses and indicated that his colleague would be prepared to

December 12, 1986

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Communications) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act, be now read a second time and referred to a Legislative Committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be presenting this Bill for debate today. I may say in looking at it that one could say it is a modest little Bill. Nevertheless, embodied in its intent and proposals are certain more basic assumptions.
Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act, will help in promoting economic renewal by ensuring financial equity and prudent administration of a very vital government service, that is, spectrum management, which provides for the effective operation of our telecommunications network and broadcasting system, and helps our enterprises to become and remain competitive.
At the same time, Bill C-3 will promote social justice by ensuring that through licence fees the costs of planning and managing the radio spectrum are shared equally among its direct beneficiaries and not borne by the general taxpayer. In other words, the people who use this service would pay for it, not the general taxpayer. The legislation will eliminate the exemptions that public sector spectrum users now enjoy from licence fees. These exemptions are unfair, since those who enjoy them often compete with private sector users who must pay licence fees.
In this electronic age, the capacity of businesses to offer services competitively often depends upon their ability to communicate quickly and efficiently. This ability depends, in turn, upon a high quality, interference free, radio frequency spectrum. The spectrum is what you might term an invisible resource, but the services which depend on it have clearly visible benefits.
Radio and television entertain and inform. Microwave and satellite facilities give us access to each other and to the world. We can be more confident of safety in the air and at sea
December 12, 1986

because the spectrum is managed effectively to permit reliable radio navigation, air traffic control, radar and two-way voice and data flow. Mobile radio on land ensures a quick response in emergencies, safety on construction sites and in frontier exploration, and efficient and economical movement of people, goods and information. Simply put, Mr. Speaker, use of the spectrum can save time, money and lives.
Since 1912 we have seen the limits of the usable spectrum expand hundreds of thousands of times. Expansion of the usable spectrum has not resulted from some physical accident. It has not come about just by chance. Rather, it has been made possible through the development and mastering of technology that exploits the particular characteristics of each of its parts. Technological innovations such as digital transmission, trunking and cellular technologies have also served to expand the capacity of the spectrum.
In addition to increases in the uses of the air waves, we have also seen vast increases in the number of users. In the past 40 years the number of radio licences in force in Canada has risen over 100 times to three-quarters of a million in 1986. In only 20 years the number of mobile radio stations alone has grown from 60,000 to over a half a million, not including the 355,000 stations licenced in the general radio or CB service.
The Government of Canada, through the Department of Communications, is given the task of ensuring the orderly development and management of the spectrum in Canada. This involves assigning appropriate positions on the spectrum to particular uses and setting corresponding equipment standards.
International agreements are often required to ensure that our spectrum needs are met. These require extensive planning and negotiation with other countries. Domestic regulatory action is also taken to ensure that the spectrum resource is shared equitably among all Canadians. The role of the Government, quite simply, is to allow as many Canadians as possible ready access to a high quality radio spectrum and all its benefits.
Technology has responded to the challenge of mastering the properties of previously unusable portions of the spectrum in order to open them up for practical use. There are new challenges, however, to which a purely technical response is inadequate. We are being called upon to manage, with fewer resources, a radio communications environment made ever more complex by new applications which marry telecommunications and computer technologies. These include digital data, mobile radio and intra-building communications. We are committed to greater efficiency and cost control. The number of person-years devoted to spectrum management has been reduced and is now less than it was 10 years ago, despite sizable increases in the licensed population.
Nevertheless, we are also committed to cost recovery. Bill C-3 has been developed to ensure that legislation affecting the
Radio Act
management and use of the spectrum in Canada is an effective tool serving government efforts to maintain the quality of, and accessibilty to, an increasingly crowded spectrum. Our objective is to recover the full cost of this management effort from all its beneficiaries. We wish to remove the exemptions that now apply to certain users and to create, through legislative reform, a more equitable environment for all spectrum users, large or small, public or private.
We have changed the radio licence fee structure significantly since 1984. Radio licence fees were increased substantially for private sector users two years ago. This was in accordance with the principle that the cost of planning and managing the spectrum resource should be borne by the beneficiaries of that effort and not by general tax revenues. Further regulatory revisions, introduced on April 1, 1986, served to make the licensing process and fee structure more responsive and equitable, a step in the regulatory reform process to which this Government is commmitted. I can report that no further general increase in licence fees is now required. Private sector users in Canada are carrying their fair share of the cost of spectrum management. However, under the current Radio Act, public sector users are not.
Public sector radio users have long enjoyed fee exempt status. Over the years this has resulted in regional and sectoral inequities. Public utilities in some parts of our country do not pay radio licence fees, while similar utilities in other parts of Canada do indeed pay. Private sector companies who pay radio licence fees are often in competition with public sector companies who do not. For example, we now have a situation where Alberta Government Telephones, an Alberta Crown corporation, competes head to head with Cantel, a private company, in the delivery of cellular mobile telephone services. Exempting government users from paying licence fees is clearly inequitable. It is also poor management. This change will spread radio licence fees evenly across Canada among 140 provincial government departments and agencies and 40 federal government departments and agencies. The total dollar value is in the order of $10 million based on available data. Government organizations which make only light use of the spectrum should be encouraged to release licences, and thus scarce spectrum resources, for other users. However, the present system creates no such incentive.
Bill C-3 would redress these problems. It would correct the regional competitive imbalances which have crept into the radio licensing system. It would ensure that all users of the spectrum pay their fair share. Its passage would result in more prudent management of government resources. The radio spectrum is a limited resource and is managed for the benefit of all Canadians no matter where they live. The Bill is intended to respond to the new reality of communications in Canada, a reality characterized by a reliance upon competitive forces and equitable management of national resources.
Fairness and equity, cornerstones of this Government's regulatory reform strategy, will be well served by Bill C-3. The common property nature of the spectrum resource requires

December 12, 1986
Radio Act
that it be managed with efficiency and every possible application of equity. It is not only reasonable that all those who benefit from government management of the radio spectrum resource should bear an appropriate portion of the cost. Our commitment to fairness and equity requires it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act and bring fairness and equity across the spectrum governed by this Act. Although the Bill is only a few lines long we should not be lulled into believing it is not important. It is very important. If passed in its present form it will have important ramifications for those government institutions which utilize radio frequencies for communication purposes.
At the present time the federal Department of Communications is charged with the responsibility of setting the rules for those who wish to use the radio spectrum in Canada for purposes other than broadcasting to the public. The Department regulates these users by means of a licence to operate at a certain frequency and power in a certain place so that there is no interference with others using the spectrum. In short, the Department is concerned with spectrum management. It is an onerous responsibility, not obvious to the ordinary Canadian, but one which impacts on the safety of their every day lives.
This is not the first time this Bill to amend the Radio Act has been introduced by the Government. During the last session of Parliament the previous Minister of Communications introduced for first reading Bill C-126, which was identical to this Bill. That Bill died on the Order Paper when the Government chose to prorogue. Why would the Government choose to introduce such a Bill on the next to last day before it prorogued? The only logical answer seems to be that it lacks a sense of timing and direction in its legislative agenda. If cost recovery is the goal it should have legislated on time.
Bill C-3 establishes a user-pay principle. Current provisions of the Radio Act exempt federal and provincial government departments and agencies, as well as certain Crown corporations, from paying radio licence fees. Bill C-3 would remove that exemption. As a result, those government departments and agencies would pay the same licence fees as a private sector user. That strikes me as being fair and equitable.
Opposition Parties are sometimes accused of being too negative in their approach to legislation introduced in Parliament. I would like to begin by highlighting some of the positive aspects of this Bill and indicating why I am in accordance with it.
The positive feature of charging government departments for radio licences is that those departments may be forced to reconsider whether they really need to occupy a radio frequency. Charging an entity for a service which has previously been provided free may force the entity to reconsider the need for the service in the first place and to become more efficient
managers. Therefore, it is possible that some Government agencies which currently hold licences but make minimal use of radio frequencies may decide to surrender those licences. As a result, a number of frequencies may be freed up for users. As the Minister pointed out, there has been tremendous growth in this sector and there is a need to free up frequencies.
The second positive aspect of Bill C-3 is that the revenues generated from the new fees to be charged to government agencies should enable the Department of Communciations to recover fully the cost of operating its radio frequency spectrum branch. Therefore, the radio frequency spectrum branch of the Department would no longer be a drain on the federal Treasury but would become fully self supporting. I certainly support that initiative.
With respect to the private sector fee increases, Bill C-3 should also please those in the private sector who have to date been paying licence fees to support the operations of the radio frequency branch of the Department of Communcations. I understand that for the year 1985-86 private users received a very hefty increase in licence fees. I am sure these users will have a sense of relief, fairness and equity at the prospect that government users of radio frequencies will now be bearing a fair share of these costs. By placing private users and government users on the same footing, Bill C-3 will reduce one advantage previously enjoyed by government, namely, the exemption from radio licence fees. For example, when a Crown corporation such as Petro-Canada communicates through radio frequencies with its drilling rigs, the corporation will now be assessed licence fees on the same basis as would a private oil company such as Texaco.
I understand that the Crown corporation known as Alberta Government Telephones has been exempt to date from paying licence fees with respect to its cellular telephone operations. The Minister alluded to that in her speech. Yet, private firms competing with Alberta Government Telephones in the same cellular telephone market have been paying radio licence fees. Bill C-3 should eliminate this particular cost advantage enjoyed by a company such as Alberta Government Telephones.
The concern I have with regard to that is that there may not be a full understanding and appreciation of the impact of these costs to Alberta Government Telephones. According to the new fee schedule which I received from the Minister's Department, this will cost Alberta Government Telephones $1,089,122. In addition, the Saskatchewan Power Corporation will be charged $59,000. In her speech the Minister indicated that Ontario pays fees while Quebec does not. The cost to Hydro-Quebec will be $437,352. The Nova Scotia Power Corporation will pay $41,180. The New Brunswick Electric Power Commission will pay $26,000. Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro will pay $25,000 and B.C. Hydro will pay $210,790. These are large sums of money. The total for the Saskatchewan Telecommunications Network will be well in
December 12, 1986

excess of half a million dollars. The Government of Saskatchewan will have to pay $695,522. The cost to the Manitoba Telephone System will be close to half a million dollars.
With those amounts of monies involved, I feel very strongly that the views of the hydro companies, telecommunciations industries and the governments upon which this will impact should be heard. For that reason I think that this Bill, although it consists of only three lines, should be examined quite carefully. The people who will be impacted should have an opportunity, through the Government's consultative mechanisms, to know exactly what the result of this Bill will be. I was informed by the Department of Communications of the amount of money involved with respect to licence fees. I hope the Minister's Department was in communication with the Departments impacted in order that they would be aware of the effect on them.
I have listed some of the positive aspects of Bill C-3, but my Party would not be doing its job as the Official Opposition if we did not point out some of the problems which we perceive the Bill may create.
One example is Section 2(3) of the Radio Act. It should be pointed out that while Bill C-3 purports to amend Section 2(2) of the Radio Act, the Bill leaves Section 2(3) of that same Act in place. Section 2(3) gives the federal Cabinet the power, on the recommendation of the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), to exempt a federal Government radio frequency user from the provisions of the Radio Act itself. The Cabinet cannot exempt a provincial Government user.
One of the objectives of Bill C-3 is apparently to provide for equality of treatment among all users of the spectrum, be they federal Government, provincial Government, or private sector. Even the Department of Communications itself will have to pay radio licence fees.
Having provided for this equality in Bill C-3, I trust that, unless the Minister of Communications has very strong reasons for doing so, she will not proceed to recommend to Cabinet the exemption of federal agencies from the Radio Act, for to do so would be to remove the equality of treatment which we are told the Bill is intended to provide. If there is no indication of this in the Bill through amendment or the inclusion of some change in Section 2(3) of the Radio Act, there is no way of assuring provincial Governments and hydro electric companies that they will never be subject to an Order in Council which could change the rules of the game, which is allowed under Section 2(3) of the Bill. I think the Minister should consider that. I want to discuss that in committee when the Bill is before it.
Although the Government indicates that the fees to be charged government users under the Bill will be calculated on the same basis as the fees already assessed to the private user, Bill C-3 does not so provide. Rather, the drafters of Bill C-3 seem content to allow the regulations to stipulate that the fee assessment will be the same. This means that even if Bill C-3 is passed-Mr. Speaker, I would like direction from the Chair. I
Radio Act
have some very important information and observations to bring to the House with respect to this Bill. As it is almost one o'clock, I ask your guidance. Shall I continue my remarks at two o'clock?
