speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the Hon. Member for Mount Royal had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I was commenting on the rather significant aspects of Bill C-3 now before the House, a measure which does not appear to be overly controversial- all three lines of it-but which will affect all Hertzian wave users in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act, reads as follows:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. Subsection 2(2) of the Radio Act is repealed and the following substituted
therefor:
"(2) Subject to subsection (3), Her Majesty in right of Canada and each province is bound by this Act."

Clause 1: This amendment sould repeal the exemption from the payment of licence fees granted to Her Majesty in right of Canada or any province.
It has been recommended that the procedure of the Department of Communications be changed so that expenditures incurred by the Department may be recovered.

Although the Government indicates that the fees to be charged government users under the Bill will be calculated on the same basis as the fees already assessed to private users, Bill C-3 does not so provide. Rather, those who drafted Bill C-3 seem content to allow the regulations to stipulate that the fee assessment will be the same. This means that even if Bill C-3 is passed, there is absolutely no assurance, other than the good will and the word of the Minister, that government and private sector users of the spectrum will be assessed licence fees calculated on the same basis. I accept the Minister's good will and her word, but it is not law. The Government could still amend the regulation to require one class of user to pay higher fees, be it the Government or the private sector.
Therefore, I hope the Government will ensure that once Bill C-3 has passed, regulations are consistent to ensure this

December 12, 1986
Radio Act
equality of treatment. I will be recommending an amendment to the effect that the revenues be capped to the cost recovery for the Department of Communications, and that fairness and equality be assured for the public and private sector. In that regard, I want to discuss in the Legislative Committee the most effective procedures as perceived by the Department of Communications, the Minister and her staff to be able to provide the equity she talked about in her presentation.
Let me deal with the revenues to be raised by the Bill. According to the recent briefings and figures that were supplied to me by the Department of Communications, I understand that the current shortfall between the amount of revenue generated by the radio frequency spectrum branch of the Department and the cost of operating that branch is approximately $10.1 million. I am also informed by officials of that Department that the Government projects that Bill C-3 will allow it to generate an additional sum of $10.1 million from federal and provincial government agencies.
I want to make two comments about those figures. First, the Minister said this morning that the calculation was not final. Second, the Department of Communications seems to hold the view that the passage of Bill C-3 will lead some government users to give up their licences, thereby reducing the amount of licence fees collected. One wonders if the Government is aware that its projections of $10.1 million in additional revenues would appear to be based on the assumption that all current government licence holders will continue to retain their licences. One also wonders whether there may be far in excess of the $10 million raised by this procedure when we consider all the new users who are presently using this service.
Second, the prediction of $10.1 million in additional revenue to be generated by Bill C-3 also fails to take into consideration that new regulations announced by the Government in its press release on June 26, 1986 will likely generate a further $2 million in revenue from Canadian municipalities. I will have more to say about municipalities later.
It is also noteworthy that the report of the Nielsen Task Force on management of regulatory programs included a graph on page 186 which showed that the radio frequency branch of the Department cost $45 million, with a revenue of only $600,000. The Department briefing indicated that only $10.1 million was needed to make the whole procedure selfsupporting. Therefore, one can only conclude that there is some confusion in government circles on exactly how much additional revenue will be generated, how much will be needed and how we can assure that this becomes strictly a cost recovery mechanism rather than an additional revenue generator for the federal treasury.
I support the Government's attempt to institute the cost recovery principle and I think it is very important that it be outlined and defined in this Bill. The Bill should include reference to capping the cost recovery that is envisaged.
I am advised by the Department of Communications personnel that they do not expect that new staff will be needed
to assess new licence fees against government agencies and Crown corporations. While I appreciate that much of the additional work can be done by programming computers, I am concerned that the Department may have overlooked one point. The point is that although the names and addresses of the government users are already on the computer file of the Department of Communications, departmental personnel may, after the passage of Bill C-3, have to go out into the field to ascertain the number of base stations and mobile units which are held by each of the government users. Since I understand that the new fee will be computed according to the number of base stations, that is, the number of headquarters, plus the number of mobile units, that is, the units in each individual car or truck, extra personnel may be needed to make these calculations. If this is not the case then it could be cleared up in a legislative committee hearing which could refine and define the procedures which are to be used to evaluate the cost to be recovered from each of the organisms that will be touched by this Bill.
[DOT] (MIO)
I hope that the Government is aware that Bill C-3 could have important budgetary consequences on certain government departments which are heavy users of radio frequency transmissions. For example, I am in receipt of figures from the office of the Minister of Communications which show that the RCMP will be faced with new licensing fees of approximately $1,012,562 as the result of the passage of Bill C-3. The RCMP was previously exempt from paying such fees. I trust that the Government will not push ahead with this Bill without considering this new drain on the resources of that agency and on the costs to the Government itself.
This is where Clause 2(3) of the Bill could be used by Government and were it could exempt this particular department, and others which I will note. It would restore the whole sense of equity and fairness. For example, the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans will receive a bill for $189,166. I do not know if that is a firm figure or otherwise. I do not know whether the Department knows that it will receive such a bill. The bill for the Department of Communications will be $27,000. As 1 have said, the bill for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will be $1,012,562. How will that affect the Force and from where will that sum be forthcoming? Will it be a new allocation or a supplementary allocation? For the House of Commons it will cost $10,860.
I would now like to deal with some of the Crown corporations on which this Bill will have an impact. With respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the impact will be $132,204. With respect to TeleGlobe Canada the bill will be $4,364. The figure for Petro-Canada will be $75,791. With respect to Canada Post, which we hope will break even, the figure will be $26,834. I have outlined the cost of a number of these initiatives in the cost-recovery program. The question is who will be paying for it? In the end it will be the hydro and utility subscribers, as well as telephone subscribers.
December 12, 1986

Although the Government in its findings and in this document indicates that the expense revenue from provincial Government departments will be $4.4 million and $2.7 million from provincial Government agencies, there are over $7 million coming from provincial Governments which have not as yet to my knowledge been calculated into their over-all budgeting procedure. I think the least we could do is allow them to let us know how they are planning to handle this situation. Will it be through an increase in user fees directly to the telephone subscriber, or will it be directly to the user of the electricity and heat that is coming through because they are using this radio frequency to communicate with their fleet of trucks? With respect to the $3 million which will have to come from federal Government departments out of existing budgets there is nothing with respect to municipalities in this legislation.
I am also advised by the office of the Minister of Communications that the passage of Bill C-3 will mean that the CBC, which was previously exempt, will have to pay more. It is a well known fact that the Government has already cut the budget of the CBC. Perhaps I am being too generous when I use the phrase "cut the budget" since it might be more accurate to say that it was savaged. Will the federal Government increase the CBC's budget to cover the cost of this new licensing fee? I will be seeking an answer to that question and others when the Bill is referred to a legislative committee.
I wonder whether provincial Crown corporations such as Hydro-Quebec have been made aware that it will face new radio licence fees to the tune of $437,000. I know that there was a short, sharp line in the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) back in February that was supposed to have advised all these organizations that they would be receiving bills with respect to radio licence fees. I do not know if they were aware of the extent of the bill. I do not know if they have made provisions for it and what is their point of view. The telephone companies in the prairie provinces which will be required to pay substantial new fees as a result of this Bill may have something important to say about it.
Thus my question is, who will pay in the end? The Minister of Finance will recover these funds into his General Revenue Fund but the provincial Governments and Hydro-Quebec will have to go to the users, that is, the taxpayers, with respect to something which is a hidden tax to the homeowner, the businessman and the private telephone subscriber. I hope the Government is aware that this housekeeping cost-recovery measure will cost, and cost us all. It will shift the tax burden once again to the provinces and to the utility companies with no cap on it in its present form.
I referred earlier to the effect this Bill will have on municipalities. I have received correspondence from the head of the municipalities of Canada and from many of the mayors to find out just what was meant in the communique which reads:
Communications Minister Marcel Masse, in a measure supportive of the Government's deficit-reduction plans, today tabled legislation that would require federal and provincial government departments and agencies, along with
Radio Act
municipalities, to pay radio licence fees on the same basis as private users, beginning April 1, 1987.
Under the Radio Act as it now stands departments and agencies of the Crown are exempt from paying licence fees. The communique goes on to explain why the Minister feels that all users of this spectrum, both public and private, should be put on an equal footing for the first time, which will equitably apportion the costs of the spectrum management among all licence users. We have little indication that there will be any change to that. The Bill is identical, all but in number, to a previous Bill.
The Ministers have changed but the present Minister answered a question in the House which leaves cause for concern and consideration again. In response to a question asked by the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau), who asked the Minister if she has been able to resolve the matter with respect to volunteer fire departments which would be required to pay individual licensing fees for their two-way radios which might have an added substantial cost to the operation of such fire departments, the Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for South West Nova for his representations on this issue. Indeed, I have received representations on the issue from a number of other Members. I should like to advise him and the House that I have decided to defer for the time being any changes to the regulations as they apply to radio licence fees for municipalities and volunteer fire departments.
These changes are quite separate and distinct from those included in Bill C-3 which applied to federal and provincial agencies and Crown corporations. They will be proceeded with. However, the changes as they affect municipalities and volunteer fire departments will not be proceeded with.
The question remains, does that mean at all or for the time being? The Minister can giggle and be as nasty as she wishes, but her answer is unclear. If she were the mayor of a municipality she would have certain concerns. If she were the head of a volunteer fire department she would have the right to a clear and unequivocal answer from the Minister and not just a snicker. That is not an answer, and I would suggest that she take her responsibilities concerning these people a little more seriously.
When the Government first introduced the Bill to amend the Radio Act, it issued the press release to which I have just referred. Was the news release misleading? Was the Minister's answer ambiguous? It does give the impression that either now or some time in the future, at the whim of the Minister, the Bill could certainly have an impact which would require municipalities to pay radio licence fees. In fact, municipalities are already paying radio licence fees pursuant to regulations issued under the Radio Act.
Bill C-3 itself does not target municipalities. Rather, it would appear that the Government intends to amend the regulations with respect to municipalities in order to require municipalities to pay fees on the same basis as private users. Municipalities are presently paying fees on a reduced basis so

December 12, 1986
Radio Act
there had better be some clarification of the equity and fairness to which the Minister referred.
There is no control over fees in this Bill. It is through regulations that municipalities have been charged fees. The intention of the Government is clearer than it would have wished it to be. Did the prior Minister of Communications indicate that municipalities should pay? Is the Government hiding this and will it spring it on municipalities later? I think the Government must come clean on this and I would like it clarified.
Some municipalities may not fully appreciate the additional costs which would be incurred. Those municipalities that use radio frequencies to communicate with garbage collectors, snow removers and street maintenance workers may receive unexpected bills from the federal Department of Communications. Furthermore, municipalities which operate their own police departments, fire departments or ambulance services may also pay more for radio licences. Based on the discussions I have had with a number of prominent mayors of Canadian municipalities, it is not at all clear to them or to me whether or not municipalities have been consulted by the Government about the proposed legislation, or that they have had their fears allayed. I would suggest that in committee, it would be much appreciated if the Minister would table any correspondence in that regard and assure the municipalities of their situation.
In order to clear up the confusion on this issue, the Hon. Member for South West Nova pointed certain things out and received an answer for the time being. I suggest that we should find out the answer once and for all as there remains some confusion about the Minister's comment that she will not proceed with the regulations for the time being. How can municipalities plan budgets?
As I said, I do wish to have this clarified but I do not wish to be obstructionist. I do not wish to cause unnecessary delay, but many people who will be touched by this Bill have concerns. I would suggest that we hear from those people as quickly as possible, as we would when dealing with any Bill that would impose unanticipated taxes or have a large impact. These people have a right to be heard.
I would also suggest that the Bill proceed to a Legislative Committee or the Standing Committee so that various provincial Government agencies or agencies such as the CBC, the RCMP and Alberta Government Telephones will have an opportunity to make representations. I do not expect that the committee's deliberations should have to be lengthy, but I do not wish to deprive interested parties of the right to appear and state their views. I would urge that this Bill be moved to committee and that deliberations take place so we may arrive at the proper decision.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Minister and to the spokesperson for the Official Opposition. I think I understand the objectives of the Government. I am a little bit at a loss, though, as to which side
the Official Opposition is on. Perhaps it is on all sides. I heard the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) compliment the Minister in the early part of her speech and then complain about a few things in the latter part of her speech. This causes me to hope that she will have many amendments to move when we get into committee and report stage.
The Minister said that this Bill will help our enterprises, enterprises meaning those that use the public airwaves, to become more competitive and that the general taxpayer will not have to pay for this. I take it from that that she meant that the general taxpayer would not have to pay for the provision of infrastructure and other services provided by the federal Government. She said that the Bill would provide more confidence in safety in the air, at sea and on the land. This causes me to raise the point about the Department of National Defence cancelling all radar, direction, air-speed and ground-speed services to commercial aircraft flying in northern Canada and the high Arctic without the knowledge of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). So much for safety in the air.
When I raised this matter with him earlier in the week, the Minister of Transport was good enough to send me a letter the next morning saying that he was looking into the matter. I suspect that he was slightly annoyed about it. I suspect that the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) did not know about it either. The Department of National Defence probably did not tell her either that these services for commercial aircraft that had been provided for several decades by the Department of National Defence would no longer be provided as of October 1 of next year.
The Minister said that in terms of domestic services, this Bill would provide for all Canadians to share equally and that it was a part of regulatory reform. I would like to raise a question about this equal sharing on the part of all Canadians. Here we have a situation of the Crown taxing the Crown. Taxpayers' money will be shifted from one pocket to the other or, more accurately, taxpayers' money will be taken out of a different pocket, in this case the municipalities pocket.
Taxpayers have at least four pockets. They have one for the federal Government, one for the provincial Government, one for the municipal Government and another for the educational system. This Bill provides that the federal Government will tell the taxpayers to take this money out of their municipal Government tax pocket rather than their federal Government tax pocket.
In response to a question put in the House by the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau) about fees to be paid by police departments, fire departments and volunteer fire departments, the Minister said that she would like to advise the Hon. Member and the House that she had decided to defer for the time being any changes to the regulations as they apply to radio licences for municipalities and volunteer fire departments. We, in our caucus, do not think that is good enough. A year from now the Minister may be promoted to a higher level, and a subsequent Minister may decide "for the time being"
December 12, 1986

has expired. Pressure on this Minister by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) may require her to decide "for the time being" has expired.
I think the Minister in her heart of hearts has no objection to building an exemption into the Bill for organizations such as police departments, municipal fire departments, volunteer fire departments, ambulances, municipal or volunteer emergency measures organizations, forest fire-fighting operations, and search and rescue operations. Why should non-profit public bodies that are set up by the taxpayers either through a municipal or a voluntary organization, for example, police departments, fire departments, volunteer fire departments, ambulance services, search and rescue operations, forest firefighting operations, have to pay for using something that already belongs to them, that is, the air waves in Canada? There should be a fee charged for the use of public air waves for private profit. I agree with that, and I think that my colleagues agree. But surely any public utility or service that does not make a profit should not have to pay, through taxes, for the air waves that they already own.
The federal authority in its provision of the infrastructure for these public utilities and volunteer organizations which operate for the public's well-being and safety has a duty to accept this as part of the service. They pay their federal taxes to provide those services. Why should it be necessary to transfer taxpayers' contributions from the federal taxpayer's pocket to a municipal taxpayer's pocket? Why should they have to pay for something they already own?
In the past few years since 1976 the same thing has been going on in transportation, and it is being repeated in this Bill. When the Government of the day established VIA Rail with a $1 item under the Estimates, VIA Rail got stuck for something like $75 million to $80 million worth of old railway passenger cars and locomotives, most of which belonged to Canadian National. About three-quarters of that money was for Canadian National cars. So here we had the spectacle of the Canadian taxpayers paying for all these railway cars and locomotives that they already owned. They paid for them a second time. That is a Conservative and Liberal version of sound business practice. I call it ripping off the taxpayers, not sound business practice.
The rail passenger action force set up by the then Minister of Transport who is now the Government House Leader (Mr. Mazankowski) not only asked the question, but strongly objected to the taxpayers paying through VIA Rail to Canadian National for property, that is, stations, trackage, that the taxpayers already owned. That was a spectacle of the taxpayers paying a second time. This started VIA Rail off with the deck stacked against it.
Again I have to say if that is the Conservative-Liberal version of sound business practice, then us socialists will have to teach them some lessons about sound, fair, business
Radio Act
practice. I find that incredible. If that was tried in the private sector, it would laugh you out of town or lock you up. But the taxpayer can be victimized a second time, and annually thereafter.
The City of Regina is taking a hard look at what will have to be done with a deficit budget, and what will have to be picked up in extra fees for the police and fire departments. No chances can be taken on the Minister's assertion in Hansard that at some future date it will not be faced with having to pay fees for the radios in their police cars, fire trucks, and ambulances. Therefore, it is taking a hard look at its budget and does not know what to budget. I heard the figures that the City of Regina would be stuck with fees of $50,000 to $100,000 for all these fees to the federal Government. Regina is part of the whole general Canadian population that owns the air waves. No profits are being made; in fact money is lost on police services, fire departments, ambulance services, search and rescue, and other types of emergency operations. The taxpayer should not be required to pay any fees for radio services using air waves that belong to all Canadians.
There is no justification for any public service that is not operating for a profit to pay for the use of the air waves. There is no justification for transferring the taxation required at the federal level for this infrastructure. The Minister mentioned the facilities that the federal Government provides, as well it should. But why transfer the taxpayers' costs of those services from the federal Government to the provincial or municipal level? Is the objective to make the federal Government and its deficit look better, and the provincial or municipal deficit look worse? It does not speak well for a Government of any political stripe to be that mean-and I hate to use the word small-for an amount of $10 million in additional revenues for the federal Government, which does not amount to very much in the total scheme of things around here.
A public utility, whether it be a telephone company or a power corporation, established for the purpose of providing a public service and meeting a public need, not for the purpose of making a profit, should also be exempt. There is a difference between Bell Canada and Alberta Tel, Saskatchewan Tel and Manitoba Tel. The publicly owned and operated telephone companies in the three prairie provinces provide a service. Any profits they make are put back into the utilities. The shareholders, namely, the people of the three provinces, are not eligible for and do not expect dividends or a return on the investment they make, through their taxes, in the telephone companies. They do not expect, ask for, or get dividends. However, in the case of Ma Bell, there are many shareholders looking for dividends or for a cut of the profits. This is why telephone services in Ontario, the Territories, and parts of Quebec cost more than they do in the three prairie provinces. They cost more because the prime imperative of Bell Canada is to make a profit. If we told Bell Canada tomorrow that it could only operate on a break even level, it would say to the

December 12, 1986
Radio Act
Governments of Ontario, Quebec and the Territories, we quit; you take it over.
This is not the case with the telephone companies in the three prairie provinces. They are not there to make a profit. They are there to provide the most economical service possible to the people of the three provinces. For the years in which they make profits, the profits go back into capital investment or, if any part thereof goes into the provincial treasuries, in turn the provincial treasuries guarantee loans when they have to go out on the capital market to borrow.
There is no comparison between Bell Canada and the telephone companies of the three prairie provinces having to pay radio fees. The Minister should agree to including in the Bill that those kinds of public utilities, as well as the ones involved in emergencies concerning the health, safety, and security of the citizenry, be exempted from fees.
The people who are shareholders in the ownership of our air waves are being asked to pay again for something they already own. Through their federal income taxes they have already paid for the various facilities of the Department of Communications. They have paid for them once. Now the Minister wants them to pay again for something for which they have already paid when it comes to infrastructure and facilities in the Department of Communications. Surely that does not make good business, economic or social sense.
When the matter is before the committee, I hope the Minister will present an amendment to exempt those functions in society. There is no plausible reason for going to those lengths.
I must confess that I do not understand why Ontario Hydro pays the fees and Quebec Hydro does not. They are both public companies with shares all over the place. I understand that Quebec Hydro may not be a Crown corporation-
It is. They both are Crown corporations.

In that case, Quebec Hydro, Ontario Hydro, Saskatchewan Hydro, and Manitoba Hydro are equal in that respect. They are public utilities. The prime principle for their existence is to provide electrical power at cost. They are not in existence to make a profit first and to provide service second. They are in existence to provide an essential public service.
It would be great if the Minister included a regulation that any power corporation, be it publicly or privately owned, which does not put its profit back into the enhancement of service, infrastructure, or capital requirements, should pay a fee. There is a fundamental conflict in the legislation.
The Minister agreed that she would defer, for the time being, any fees which apply to radio licences for municipalities and volunteer fire departments. I accept her word and believe her. She does not want to charge them a fee. Why not have it included in the Bill? I am sure the Minister has received representations from the urban and municipal associations, fire departments, and police departments across the country. It is
nothing more than financial nit-picking. The Government may feel that it is at the bottom of the revenue barrel. However, it is boring a hole through the bottom of the barrel trying to get below the bottom of the bottom, to get a few million dollars in revenue which will make no difference whatsoever.
If it is the desire of the Minister's officials to show that the Department is breaking even, tough cookie. If their objective is to indicate that the Department is paying its own way, at the expense of municipalities, volunteer fire departments, search and rescue operations, and forest fire-fighters, their objective is badly skewed and their priorities are misplaced. They cannot have it both ways. They cannot make taxpayers pay more than once for the services they receive.
It is futile and improper to transfer a tax burden from the federal authority to a municipality. It would be bad enough to do that to a province. However, to transfer those costs from the federal authority to the provincial or municipal authorities surely is not only improper but an evasion of federal responsibility. The federal Government is in charge of Canadian public air waves. Therefore I agree with the Minister that it is its responsibility to administer efficiently and fairly those air waves. There is no argument about that. Surely it is not fair to transfer the cost of a proper and constitutionally based responsibility from the federal Government to a provincial Government, a municipal Government, or a non-profit organization. It does not stand up to examination. It is patently wrong and totally unnecessary.
If we were talking about hundreds of millions of dollars or billions of dollars, I suppose one would be hard put to object in light of the government deficit, that is, if one lost a lot of sleep about the deficit. I do not lose a lot of sleep about it. About 80 per cent of that deficit we owe ourselves. The Government borrows money from us and pays it back through our Canada Savings Bonds, guaranteed investment certificates, treasury bills, bonds or whatever.
There is no fiscal or financial imperative here for the Department of Communications to be trying to make taxpayers pay again for something they already own, and I mentioned the situation of VIA Rail and the CNR. Asking the taxpayers to pay a second time for something they already own is not even funny, but it is sort of endemic in every department. Public domain is the property of the public.
When you apply the principle of user pay across the board, started by the late unlamented Otto Lang, which the Conservatives decried as vociferously as we did-probably even more so because there were more of them-to something that already belongs in the public domain it is self-defeating. It is self-defeating in the sense that you are saying to the people of Canada that the air waves belong to them. Then you are telling them that, while they have paid federal tax to cover infrasture and the cost of the Department of Communications, they now have to pay again through their municipalities. They will pay fees for their little radios, police cars, fire trucks,
December 12, 1986

volunteer fire departments and search and rescue operations unless those are operated by the federal Government and are exempt.
I think of the hundreds and hundreds of hours put in by volunteer pilots with their aircraft searching for downed aircraft. Why charge them a fee for their radios?
Agreed.

Are we that desperate that we have to nitpick and pick up every spare copper that the federal Treasury can get? That does not say much for the greatness of the minds of those in the Government, and it does not speak well for the officials in the Minister's Department.
I hope the Minister of Communications will rise in her place and tell us that she does have at least one, preferably two or three amendments, that would put in practice her own view. I believe her and I accept her word that she has considered the representations made by the urban municipal associations, police and fire departments. I hope she defers this Bill for the time being. I want to say to the Minister though, as sincerely as I can, that her statement really is not good enough. To make sure that nobody will charge fees on these kinds of public services, public utility operations, one must put it into the legislation. I, and I believe my colleagues and my caucus, have no objections to those paying a fee who use the public airwaves to make a private profit. They should pay a fee because they are renting part of the airwaves. We have no objection to that. But you do not pick on ambulances, fire trucks and police cars. For God's sake use your heads over there if you are capable. This is so crazy that it would be laughable, except that it is so bad in principle.
Surely the Government has no other alternative but to extend the legislation in a small way, and that will not in any way affect the Government's ability to collect revenues from radio and television stations. The Minister wept tears over Cancom, a private telecommunications company in Alberta having to pay this fee while the Alberta Government Telephones did not. My hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal, did not think that was very nice. I am subject to correction on this, but I think Cancom is part of the CNCP operation and a few other fast buck operators. If they want to use the public airwaves for private profit, then they should damn well pay a fee. Why should Alberta Government Telephones, which the taxpayers bought and paid for, have to pay a fee-
One million dollars worth.

-just because Cancom does? The Government telephone systems in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are not there to make a profit, they are there to provide a service. That is why they are publicly owned and that is why our telephone rates are lower than in the rest of Canada. That is a return on the taxpayers investment in those three provinces.
Radio Act
This Bill flies in the face of good fundamental principle. The federal authorities are responsible for what comes under federal jurisdiction, and through the general tax system collect moneys to cover the costs of the Minister's Department and all other Departments. The taxpayers pay for that. Why then turn around and ask taxpayers, through their police departments or city councils or whatever, to pay a second time? I wish I had a spare million dollars because I would take the Minister to Federal Court about double taxation. We could have a lot of fun with that. It is just so bad in principle that I hope the Minister will agree that there needs to be an exemption built into the Bill for municipalities, police departments, fire departments, volunteer fire departments and search and rescue operations that are not federally operated. The Department of National Defence is already exempt, as it should be when it comes to search and rescue. In those instances they should pay a fee. Charge them $5 or $10 for each flight for the use of radios when flying Ministers, or even me, somewhere.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, all you are doing is taking money from one department to another. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to comment on Bill C-3, a very thin Bill in content and principle. It looks so innocuous yet it has incredible implications for the taxpayers of Canada. It is the intention of the NDP to move with some haste to
complete second reading of this Bill and get the Bill into committee. As so many people have indicated, it is important that amendments be made and that the Government be straightened out on this issue.
By and large Bill C-3 will remove the exemption from payment of radio licence fees now enjoyed by federal and provincial governments and their agencies. The Government expects to raise in the order of $10 million a year through this Bill. That money will come from public bodies such as Alberta Government Telephones, Quebec Hydro, Telesat, Petro-Canada, SaskTel and Manitoba Tel. The Department of Communications tells us that licence fees will now range from $5,000 a year to as high as $1 million from agencies such as Alberta Government Telephones. Of course, that cost will be passed on to the various ratepayers, which means the cost of telephone service in Alberta and other western provinces will increase.
In fact, while no one has made the point, this Bill discriminates against western Canada. The Bill identifies western Canadian Crown corporations and government telephone systems and adds to their costs. The lion's share, as is often the case, of this $10 million in additional revenue will come from hard pressed western provinces. This is one more example on a growing list of federal government initiatives which discriminate against western Canadians.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), indicated, additional fees will be levied on a number of organizations. What we should be doing is considering why the Radio Act originally exempted public broadcasters. There were and still are very strong arguments against the Crown taxing the Crown. The public owns the air waves already. Is it appropriate to expect public agencies and organizations oriented toward public service to now pay to use the air waves they already own? We say this is an inappropriate form of taxation. Radio licence fees are paid so that public property, the air waves, can be soundly managed in the public interest. Certainly the use of air waves should be regulated, but should taxpayers be required to pay for the use of their own property?
The federal Government, of course, is using this mechanism to reduce the deficit. In other words, Canadian taxpayers are going to be asked to pay for the use of something they already own so that the Government can collect millions of dollars in order to reduce the federal deficit. Yet in a sense all the Government is doing is transferring the cost to other jurisdictions. I suspect you are asking why I say that. I want to read from a magazine called Forum, a publication on communications for those involved in municipal Government. In its September-October issue of this year it said that this Bill, and I quote:
-would require municipalities to pay radio licence fees on the same basis as private users beginning April 1, 1987 (for police, fire and emergency services). Former Communications Minister Marcel Masse stated that the proposed amendments to the Radio Act are in keeping with the Government of Canada's deficit-reduction plans as outlined in the Finance Minister's November 1984 Economic Statement and May 1985 Budget.
December 12, 1986

Municipal leaders have commented that the proposed amendments are inappropriate insofar as they are aimed at essential public services.
That is a critical point. They are talking about police protection, fire protection and emergency services. Those organizations will now be taxed by the federal Government to use what they already own. Does that make any sense? Is that logical? No on both counts.
The chairman of the Task Force on Financing Municipal Governments, Mr. Herb Taylor, said Canadian municipalities must do everything they can to encourage the Government to reconsider this very punitive method of deficit reduction on the backs of our policemen, firemen and emergency service workers.
It is reasonable to suggest that if the Government is doing this to raise $10 million a year, surely that is an example of being penny wise and pound foolish. If the Government wants to raise $10 million, may I simply suggest two other areas which would cause an awful lot less pain, be an awful lot more equitable, and would be considered by all Canadians to be a very prudent move.
One of these would be to reform the tax system so that corporations which, in some years, have profits of hundreds of millions of dollars, pay some tax. Mr. Speaker, I know you would think that surely to goodness corporations in Canada which are profitable do pay tax. In fact, there are nearly 80,000 corporations in Canada which make a considerable profit each year, in some cases hundreds of millions of dollars, that do not pay a single cent in income tax. If these corporations paid their fair share of taxes, not only would we make up the $10 million a year which this Bill is attempting to collect, but we would collect billions more.
I understand that later today we may hear a statement by one of the Ministers on the Port-Cartier prison. This is the prison which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wanted to build in his constituency against all the recommendations of every group and individual concerned with the penal system in Canada. Putting it in his constituency will cost Canadian taxpayers in excess of $41 million. In other words, if it was built where it should be built, we would save $41 million. If all this incredible, punitive legislation is designed to do is raise $10 million in an effort to reduce the deficit, surely that is silly and ought to be changed.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. Some time ago I made representations to the Minister on behalf of the volunteer fire departments of Canada. It has been proposed by her Department that volunteer fire departments be required to pay individual licensing fees for their two-way radios. This would have added substantial costs to the operations of the volunteer fire departments. Has the Minister been able to resolve the matter and continue the previous practice of charging one licensing fee?
Today the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) is bringing in legislation which will levy considerable additional fees on volunteer fire departments, volunteer ambulance

If the Government wants to raise funds for deficit reduction, surely there are more appropriate ways which would have the support of the people of Canada, such as corporate tax reform.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking my colleagues for putting the process in motion so that we may have expeditious passage of this Bill today. I do wish to speak to the amendment which of course would, in effect, remove the very heart of the Bill. It would prevent us from increasing the rate of the federal sales tax in the way Clause 5 outlines. The motion put by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), if passed, would cost the Consolidated Revenue Fund $1.1 billion to $1.25 billion according to my calculations.
I know Hon. Members on all sides of the House want to see the Government of Canada give solid leadership in dealing with the deficit. Of course, this package of excise tax increases must be passed in order to come to terms with government expenditures and to continue our resolve to decrease the deficit.

December 12, 1986
Excise Tax Act
I know Hon. Members are aware of the considerable success we have had in meeting our target of decreasing expenditures. If it had not been for some unforeseen calamities that have occurred in the economy, we would have been right on target. Because of the calamities, including the agricultural situation and the price of oil and gas, we have had to look to new ways of raising revenue. Of course, that is what Clause 5 of this Bill does.
The federal sales tax increase of 1 per cent contained in this Bill would raise between $1.1 billion and $1.25 billion next year. As well, because of this Bill, we will not be required to increase income taxes any further than we have to date and we will not have to increase corporate taxes or customs charges and duties.
We are going through a process of tax reform. This process will look at the federal sales tax system to which the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap is speaking. If we can bring in a broader based federal sales tax, we may be able to decrease the level of taxation even further than that of which the Hon. Member is thinking after we have finished with tax reform. Until then, of course, it is imperative that the Bill as written, including Clause 5, be passed.
Federal sales tax reform will do something for which the people of Canada have waited decades. It will put in place a fair system. As we all know, federal sales tax is now applied to commodities and to manufacturing but not to the other two-thirds of the economy, the service sector. We would like to bring down the high rate of federal sales tax and spread it across a wider base. That will be part of tax reform, together with the lowering of marginal rates of personal income tax and corporate tax. It is very important that we do that.
If we did away with the federal sales tax entirely, my calculations indicate that personal income taxes would have to be increased by almost 50 per cent at the lower end. There simply would not be enough income at the top end to make up the difference. The Hon. Member is not suggesting a total removal of the federal sales tax, but theoretically, if there were no federal sales taxes, we would have to load revenue production on to the personal income taxes.
In this particular case, $1.1 billion is about one-twelfth of the problem. If we are to raise the $1.25 billion which could very well be raised through Clause 5 through the personal income tax route instead, we would have to raise taxes not only at the high level but at the middle level and that would be unacceptable given our present tax rate, particularly while the Government is absolutely determined to decrease the levels of personal income tax after tax reform.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: What about corporation tax? What would you do about that?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Corporate tax as well will be studied. In corporate tax reform, we must look at the tax preferences and deductions that are in place as well as the tax losses and all of the things that make it more difficult for us to receive the
revenues from the corporate sector that we believe we should receive. All of that is being looked at in the context of tax reform.
I welcome the Hon. Member's amendment in the sense that it is forcing us to think about in which direction we should go with the mix in our tax system. I also welcome the fact that all Hon. Members have agreed to give this Bill speedy passage. However, I must say that until the tax system is reformed, it is important that we not break from the direction this Bill is taking us. This Bill will give us the revenue required over the next year or two to put in place a more comprehensive and effective regime.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this Bill provides for a federal sales tax credit, an innovative and very important reform. It helps to reduce the regressive effect of a sales tax increase on low-income Canadians. As we went through the Bill in committee, there were many good questions put on this matter. We found out that with the average increase of 1 per cent per capita in federal sales tax, a person earning $15,000 or less annually would pay about $25.30 more, but we will give a $50 credit per adult. We are not just making a slight gesture toward people in that income bracket, but more than compensating them for the increased taxes they might have to pay.
Moving further and looking at the $25 per child, for a family including a wife, husband, and four children, there will be a credit of $200. From the calculations that I have, that more than compensates-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: It is $150.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
It is $25 per child, plus $50 per adult for the example of the prepayment of the child tax credit. The Hon. Member is quite correct that it is $150 for the example that I gave for the federal sales tax credit.
I am grateful that Members on all sides of the House are taking an interest in the question of taxation. We wish to have all the ideas produced in the next six months in a very intensive way so that our tax reform will be effective.
It is my hope, and it is in the spirit of the amendment that over-all federal sales tax levels will be able to be diminished as a result of the BTT or some variant of it that we can bring in through tax reform.
Finally, we must remember that the over-all thrust of this legislation is to help us continue on track with decreasing the deficit. That is what has given Canadian people the confidence to invest in this economy and create the thousands of jobs that have been created. It has also given us confidence in our dollar, and kept our interest rates at a moderate level. If we do not come to terms with the deficit, we will find that our interest rates will be so high that our job creation will start to fall back, and the strength and the great confidence in our economy will dwindle.
December 12, 1986

Over-all this is a measure aimed at controlling the deficit which will do so in a way that is not regressive.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to talk about this particular section and what it means in terms of the over-all changes in the sales and excise taxes which are contained in Bill C-14.
I asked the Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) a question in the House today about why the Government was giving yet another gift to the very wealthy Canadians by allowing the lifetime capital gains tax exemption to be partly free of the minimum tax. The Hon. Minister gave many irrelevant answers. He did refer to the sales tax credit. But what he did not say was that on the one hand we give a very small credit to families under very limited circumstances at the same time that we are increasing their cost of living by the increase in the sales tax which came into force on April 1, 1986. On the other hand we are giving very generously, because it turns out that the one income that people can have which will be partially exempted from the minimum tax, which I think most Canadians feel should be subject to the minimum tax, is going to be capital gains. Most capital gains income is earned or gained in some other way by people who are among the top 5 per cent of income earners in the country. So those people get a gift at Christmas from the Government-and it will be dealt with next week-and at the same time we are putting up the general sales tax from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. What this Bill does is to simply confirm what the Government did effective last April 1.
The motion moved by the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is to delete Clause 5 of the Bill. Clause 5 of the Bill has the purpose of increasing the sales tax to 15 per cent on wine and liquor, to 8 per cent on certain other products, and to 12 per cent on the sale price of most goods covered by the manufacturers sales tax.
Our concern is that the Government has chosen for the third time in a row to use a regressive means of taxation for raising revenues in its quest to fight the deficit. A regressive form of taxation is one that bears more heavily on people of modest incomes than it does on people who are wealthy. In other words, we are fighting the deficit on the backs of ordinary Canadians.
The figures are quite convincing, and I wish to read a couple into the record. In the February 26 Budget the sales tax increase for an average family will add about $150 to their cost of living. On top of that there is a cigarette and alcohol increase which will add about $20. The 3 per cent surtax which will be borne for the first time by average Canadians will add $170. The total is $340. In the Budget of May, 1985, there was $ 150 added by the broadening of the sales tax base. There was $75 added by the increase in the cigarette and alcohol tax.
There was $50 added by the increase in the gasoline tax. There were other increases which have been read into the record on a number of occasions in this House which bring the total increase for the average family to $512.50. I believe that
Excise Tax Act
we were estimating for a family in the $30,000 to $35,000 income range. In the November, 1985 Economic Statement there was a sales tax increase which at that time added $150 to the tax burden of the average family. In addition, it raised oil and gas prices by $200. It raised unemployment insurance premiums by $102. The total over the three Budgets plus the Economic Statement was $1,304.50.
The New Democrats have put those figures on the record, they have been communicated to the ministry, they have been put out through the press, and not once have those figures been challenged. I believe that is because the ministry accepts that our calculations are accurate for an average family with an income of $30,000 or $35,000 a year.
How much does that family benefit, if at all, from the sales tax credit which is being proposed? Well, none at all, because the sales tax credit will come into force for families with up to $15,000 a year of gross income. By the time it reaches a family of four, their eligibility for any sales tax credit will be extinguished when they hit an income of $18,000. In addition, the amount of the sales tax credit is all of $150 for a family of four with an income of $15,000 a year, which is 1 per cent of their income, not a heck of a lot. It disappears very quickly. For example, people in my constituency who are living at the poverty line for a major urban community like Ottawa, which is in the order of $20,000, will pay extra sales tax and will not receive a nickel's worth of benefit from the sales tax credit, which has been introduced in complementary legislation by the Government, and which we will be looking at next week.
I am particularly concerned by the fact that the Government in the Budget statement last February stated that it recognized that sales tax is a regressive tax unless something is done to soften the blow. In principle, it said what we have been saying, which is that sales tax cannot be increased unless measures are brought in to ensure that it does not bear as harshly on poor people and people with modest incomes as it does on people who are very wealthy. In principle, we are saying the same thing.
We are moving to delete this particular increase in sales tax precisely because the Government failed to follow up its principle with something practical to recognize what we mean. Since November of 1985, in the last 25 months, we have had one increase in the sales tax of $ 150 for the average family, a second increase in sales tax of $150 and now a third increase in sales tax of $150. There have been increases on cigarettes and alcohol which amounts to close to $100. There have been gas tax increases of $50. These are all taxes that tend to be regressive. The total of these various taxes would be in the order of $700.
What have we had to counter that? We have had one sales tax credit. Did the Government do anything to protect ordinary low-income families from the sales tax increase in November, 1984? Not at all. Did it do anything to protect those families from the sales tax increase and the gas tax

December 12, 1986
Excise Tax Act
increase in the 1985 Budget? Not at all. All it did was bring in something which in a modest way will reach a very limited group of families who are really very poor. They need far more to make ends meet than the sales tax credit which accompanies the sales tax increase.
When we debated the issue the other day in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, I made constructive suggestions. I had heard what was suggested by the National Council of Welfare, that the sales tax credit should be in the order of several hundred dollars for a family of four rather than $150. In fact I moved that the sales tax credit should be $200 per adult, that is, $400 for a couple or a single parent with a child, and $100 per child beyond that. It could be phased out between $15,000 and $28,000 per year for a family of four. If implemented, it would ensure a substantial measure of progressivity in terms of the application of sales tax.
I see that my time is about up. The Government is talking about bringing in a business transfer tax. It will be a hidden form of federal sales tax reaching many areas which are not taxed right now. It is saying that we should not worry about the regressivity factor because even though it is taxing almost everything one can look at, buy, consume, or get service from, it will have some kind of tax credit to offset the effect on people with modest incomes.
I do not think the Conservatives have awakened to the fact that $20,000 these days is not a heck of a lot of money on which to raise a family. The Government is giving its blueprint for the future sales tax credit with the BTT. If this is the model it chooses, it will be inadequate. This is why we are saying the particular clause should be deleted. The Government is wrong to be increasing sales tax year after year without taking adequate provision to ensure that people with low and modest incomes, working Canadian families, are in fact protected and not hit by a regressive tax levy that they can ill afford to pay.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, if the Government can give a gift to wealthy people by exempting them, at least partially, from a minimum tax on their capital gains, it should be able to do it progressively and equitably for ordinary Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have some comments to make on this amendment. First of all, we have here a political party that promised, during the last election campaign, that it would not raise taxes but reduce them, and today, if we look at sales tax alone, we have already had three increases: 1 per cent in November 1984, 1 per cent in May 1985 and 1 per cent in 1986.
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister appeared before the Committee and when he spoke this afternoon in the House, he was constantly referring to the sales tax credit for families with annual incomes of $15,000 or less. First of all, these incomes are below the poverty level, so the tax credit is not
really adequate. I think that these people, with the meager $50 they will be getting ... It is regrettable that the Government should burden people in this way by increasing taxes. Although it says it is refunding money to poor families, Mr. Speaker, with some simple arithmetic it is easy to figure out that for every 1 per cent increase in sales tax, this means an increase of $175 for a family with two children. So if we take the last three sales tax increases, we get a total of $525, and the tax credit referred to by the Minister would then add up to $150. So a family, a couple with two children and an annual income of $15,000 has had to pay $375 more in federal sales tax since September 1984.
Mr. Speaker, this is a situation we cannot accept, and maintaining the position we took on second reading, before the Committee and this afternoon as well, we intend to vote against the Bill. The Minister also referred to tax reform. We have been waiting for his proposals for some time, because we are anxious to know what they contain, what exactly the Government is going to propose. Up to now, we have not had much more than grand statements and window dressing. Everyone wants tax reform, but it all depends what kind.
Will it mean that, for instance, the Income Tax Act will be simplified or will the reform apply to all tax legislation? Will Canadians be able to make some sense of all this and realize what it is going to cost them, what a tax is, because today, there is no way we can make any sense of all this. For instance, not long ago, in fact last Saturday, we read in the Montreal Gazette about a small business, Alexander Ceramic Studio, which, because it had exceeded the $50,000 limit for business turnover, automatically became subject to federal sales tax. The owner of the business could no longer keep up with his competitors, and he actually lost money, first because of the additional financial outlay because he had to pay the tax retroactively, and second, he lost customers because he had to charge federal sales tax, while his competitors next door did not because they had not yet reached the $50,000 ceiling, and so, to get out of this mess, he had to reduce sales so that he would stay under the $50,000 limit.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that in the tax reform process all these things will be taken into account and in connection with the famous business tax which the Conservative Government is getting ready to introduce, I hope it will keep in mind all those small businesses which, once that tax has come into effect, will need to have a license, to report and to be subjected to all the redtape and accounting that such a tax will entail.
A tax reform should lead to a reduction in paperwork, but we have a tax here which will increase the paperwork since at least 500,000 small businesses will probably have to comply.
I therefore urge this Government to recognize that very special situation and take into consideration the last budget.
In committee, Mr. Speaker, we received a brief from the National Anti-poverty Organization. According to the figures published by the National Welfare Council, couples with two children having an income of about $20,000, which is below
December 12, 1986

the poverty line in many Canadian urban centres, will pay 1.3 per cent of their family income to cover the extra cost of the sales tax and excise tax increases provided for in the 1985-86 budget. Because very often in their speeches, Government Members when talking about the sales tax credit refer only to the 1 per cent in the last budget. But with the whole package, the 1985 and 1986 budgets, we will find that this meager $50 is not enough to cover that tax, especially for families with income below $20,000.
What about those with incomes of $22,000, $25,000? That is where the whole question lies, Mr. Speaker. It is my view that the Government was fully aware of that when it decided to grant an income tax credit for families with income below $15,000 it knew very well it wanted to set a limit. That was no doubt a noble gesture to hide the true intention, this Government's real objective with all those tax increases.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to support this amendment, and I would like to add that there is one amendment that deals with the whole issue of the price of wine. We are becoming increasingly aware that we have our own wine industry here in Canada. We are starting to make good Canadian wines. There are Canadian vintners, and I think the Government should realize this and perhaps abolish sales tax altogether on wine produced in Canada.

average family. The trouble is that it comes on top of $1,300 in sales tax increases since November of two years ago. It is this Government's philosophy to keep reducing the effect of tax on the rich and increasing the effect of tax on low and middle-income people.

This philosophy of the Government is different from the philosophy that we heard about some years ago, which was to trickle down. This is a philosophy of trickle up. There will be a little Mickey Mouse sales tax credit to the poor which will not come near matching what has been taken away from them in these regular sales tax increases. For the middle-income people, there will be no tax credit. The ones who have more money than they need to spend, the ones with really high income levels, will not mind paying these sales and excise tax increases. They are gaining on the income tax cuts and the increasing loopholes, such as the loopholes being made for more and more money going to fewer and fewer people through the capital gains tax relief by flipping property and playing real estate games. That sort of tax will be made more free to the really rich, and they will not mind paying 1 per cent extra on the ordinary necessities of life.
The pretended philosophy of the Government is that if we scoop money from the poor and give it to the rich then the rich will create jobs. That philosophy is not working, Mr. Speaker. Notwithstanding the statistics that the Government manipulates regarding jobs, the working people in this country as a whole are growing poorer. The rich do not spend in the same way as the poor. The rich spend a good deal of their money on luxuries, many of them imported. That does not create jobs in Canada. They spend their money travelling abroad. That does not create jobs in Canada. They probably send $10 billion or $20 billion every year out of this country in investments. There is no evidence that those billions of dollars created by the work of Canadians sent abroad by the rich, who have been able to collect them, create jobs in Canada. This philosophy of trickle up is making the country poorer.
What we have is a warning indication from some of the established groups in our country who provide a sort of monitoring, a sort of check on what is going as a result of these regular increases in the sales tax. The quarterly economic review published by the Department of Finance shows that in April and May, 1986 the disposable income of Canadians fell by 2 per cent. The Conference Board of Canada agrees that consumer spending will be slowed by the Conservative tax increases.
The consumers in the great, great majority in Canada are the low and middle-income people. It is those consumers whose failure to keep up the level of spending that our credit economy looks for who are causing a slowdown in the economy. Their disposable income is decreasing, the effect of which is beginning to depress the economy. If people cannot spend, then people cannot work to sell. If no one is buying, the stores do not buy and workers are laid off. This is how sales tax hits

December 12, 1986
Excise Tax Act
the country as well as hitting the low income and middle income people.
It would be well worth while if the people who rule this country, the people on the other side of the House, would pay attention to the statements put out by the bishops of the Roman Catholic Church three years ago in which they advocated what they called the preferential option for the poor. Their argument has a basic strong logic: A country that looks after the needs of its poorest people will find that the needs of its richest people are also looked after. It does not work the other way around. A country that rigs the tax laws the way this Government is doing, so as to take from the poor and give to the rich with a sort of vague promise that the rich will use that money to create jobs for the poor-a country that scoops from the poor to give to the rich-is ruining its own economy. It has happened many times before in history. We can see it in front of our eyes in Canada under the misguided philosophy of this Government.
That is why I support this motion to delete the 1 per cent sales and excise tax increase from this Bill, because it will not help Canada. It will bring a little more revenue to the Government perhaps at the beginning but by depressing the spending power of the vast majority of Canadians by depressing the market, a dependence on their spending power, it will cause greater troubles for our country. I ask Hon. Members to think about what they are doing this time. Two years ago it could be taken as excusable perhaps because we had a new Government, perhaps it did not know what it was doing, but by now it cannot use this excuse-

During those two years Conservatives have taken twice as much through sales and excise tax increases as they have through income tax increases; $6.7 billion as opposed to $3.3 billion. Those tax increases were not paid mainly by the rich but rather by middle-income earners. It is the poor and middle-income earners who are being hit by this Government. Not only will they suffer immediately and directly, the country as a whole will suffer unless the Government wakes up to the harm it is doing.

Mr. Speaker, we just heard an NDP Member say that the Government perhaps did not know what it was doing two years ago but today we can no longer make that accusation; the Government now knows what it is doing. However, I want to go on record as saying I totally disagree with anyone who suggests the Government knows what it is doing. I want everyone to know that before I give the rest of my remarks.
As we discuss this amendment to Bill C-14, it is important to know the commitments that those people across the way, who do not know what they are doing, made to the people of Canada before the last election. They made several promises as you will recall. I have raised those on one or two occasions in the past. They are listed in the book of 338 Tory promises, a copy of which anyone can have if they write to me, no postage stamp necessary, requesting a copy of the book of 338 Tory promises.
As I was saying, on the page dealing with small business it says that the Tories were to reduce the level of taxation facing small business and the complexity of the tax system with which they must cope. I know you want to know if it was the Tories who made that promise. The answer is yes. That is one thing the Conservative Party promised to do. What do we see instead? We see budgetary measures which mean tremendous increases not only for families but for small businesses such as the corner grocery store and small manufacturers. They all have to pay increased taxes as a result of the Government's budgetary measures.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), indicated to me earlier today that since the Government came to office the tax increases amount to something in the order of $3 billion. Not bad considering they were telling small businesses they were not going to face a tax increase.

If we look at the average and especially the cumulative impact of these taxes, we see that there is a broadening of the sales tax base. In other words, it means that the average Canadian, people like you and me, Mr. Speaker, it means that our constituents will now have to pay tax on certain items that were previously exempt.
Obviously, this is going to create problems for a great many people, for small businesses and especially for families on middle and low incomes.

We note as well the increase in alcohol and tobacco excise taxes. The amendment before us would remove that increase. Among other things, the tax on wine was increased from 14 per cent to 15 per cent. That is enough to drive a person to drink.
It is extremely frustrating to look at what the Conservatives are doing to the average Canadian. For example, let me bring to your attention, as I think I may have before, the cost of these new taxes and who is going to pay for them. A couple with two children making $15,000 a year will have to pay an extra $255 in taxes. Do you think that family has an extra $255? If they do, which they likely do not, I am sure they do not want to give it to the Tories, particularly when one considers their record.
You will know, because I brought it to your attention in the House earlier this week, that the Government spent $2.6

million for the Shamrock Summit in Quebec City, and the emphasis is on the first syllable. The Shamrock Summit saw five jets flying from Ottawa to Quebec City carrying one Minister each. I know they were Cabinet heavyweights but surely they could have doubled up. I know the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), who is in charge of watching the purse-strings, is concerned about that kind of activity by his colleagues. He drives back and forth from London in his car, and he would not want to see others flying in jets all over the place.
Then we hear the Government is going to pay the legal bills of a Member of this House amounting to $350,000. Why? Who knows. I see the junior Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty). He should know about wasteful government expenditures. He is well versed on the topic, and a participant, too. The Minister of State for Finance should know that this move to pay a former Minister's legal bills is without precedent.
I have a lot more to say on unnecessary government expenditures, such as the $ 1 million spent on the Far East trip by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but given the sense of fair play which the Liberal Party has always had, I do not want to delay the debate unduly. Given the festive season and the co-operation which is developing in this House, I think I will end my remarks and merely ask all Members to vote for the amendment which would stop these tax increases from going ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would urge all Members and of course you yourself to vote in favour of the amendment that would reduce the incredible tax increases that the Conservatives want to impose on the Canadian people.
